text_translated_detailed: A pearl fleet to Coromandel, dated the 7th of July, is mentioned—a separate extract of which is enclosed herewith. The confidence and friendship of the Company toward the Teuver [local ruler] and the obligation which the Company owed to him from the previous years' Tutucoryn war has emboldened this free lord to take up public arms against the Nayak of Tanjore, which has succeeded so well for him through the poor and effeminate governance of the Tanjore prince that he has conquered and taken all the lands from Rameswaram to the river Nagapattinam, and in the upper lands even to the capital of the Nayak itself. Whether he will now be able to maintain himself, time will reveal. In any case, this success has elevated him so much that he is beginning to conduct himself quite disrespectfully toward the Honored Company, for previously, and even last year, he always respected the Honored Company in his letters and communications above himself, but now he commands the Honored Company in his letter to send him yearly a tusked elephant as a sign of alliance, in order to make himself thereby even more formidable among his neighbors. He has also done much wrong to various Ceylonese merchants who were trading in his lands, having even shamefully beaten and struck with mules a Jaffna-Patnam burgher in place of payment, without our ever being able to obtain any satisfaction. His lands have also been greatly enriched through the Tutucoryn war with many weavers and other useful craftsmen and merchants, so that under the guise of helping us, he has taken very good care of his own affairs and made great profit. How these inhabitants have submitted themselves to the Company and we have undertaken in the name of the Honored Company to protect them is evident from two special transcripts of the original oaths, such as you will see in the authenticated copies enclosed herewith. Please be so kind as to examine them, to which we humbly defer. At the northernmost landscape of Errauwre, which is separated by an inlet of the sea, and where in the north the jurisdiction of Battecalo ends, borders another desolate marshy infertile land named Tambencarrewarre, provided with salty marshy pools, thickets, wholly unfruitful fields without fresh water on the seacoast, therefore wholly or very little inhabited. This land the aforementioned dessave has also traveled through and found very few or almost no people therein. It is above the seacoast 4, 5, or 6 miles inland inhabited by wild, rough, very black and brutal people named Wedas, others say Bedas. These all sustain themselves mostly by hunting without sowing or planting. Their food is wild boar and elk meat and honey. Lying beyond this landscape, going around the upper lands of Battecalo and Cotjaer to the wild Wannias northward, this people also, who had joined themselves to the aforementioned Vidauw, and who would have struck down the aforementioned sergeant and 22 soldiers, still stand as yet sufficiently under no one's authority, nor do they allow anyone to pass through their land without having a guide from them. text_translated_detailed: The young leader seized Raja by the neck, and Raja, through the help of his people, got the opportunity to flee again to his mountain or certain stronghold where it is said Raja's treasures are kept, named Gallapetij Wadder, where Raja is now said still to reside and his war force, consisting of 3,000 lascars who had come to the lower lands, has recovered, and already a good number of the conspirators (some rumors speak of about 300) are said to have been put to death, among them the old dessave of the seven corles [districts], who had been very devoted to us. Meanwhile, the news coming to Raja of the capture of our people immediately gave orders that they not be brought above with further displeasure, as it is reported to us for certain that those who had violated his word should bear their punishment, renewing again especially his order that all those who had departed from the upper lands should not come above, or would be immediately killed. These traitors, as aforesaid, having succeeded in their design at Carandore, came with the people of the Bilgal and other corles, who had been forced to them through the loss of Arandore that had befallen them, forth from Arandore to Ruanelli, thinking that the lieutenant dessave had departed to Saffragam, and that the lieutenant in the palisade would be as ready as the other. However, the lieutenant dessave stood to go to Saffragam that day when he received the news that ours were besieged at Arandore, and as he had no thoughts of surrendering that post, he wrote to the Council at Colombo that they should order him freely and not hasten to second him, as he had no concern at all, and could very well await their relief, as the Council indeed stood to send there, first the Captain the Master and thereafter Captain St. Martin to lead the force, to secure our people and to do what was necessary. These, being at Ruanelle and receiving the news that Arandore was lost, held their stand there, as also the enemy held still, hoping to make ours yield by talking in some way. But seeing no chance to deceive ours, they began to scold greatly that we had murdered their envoys, urging our lascars to turn away from us and to let themselves be handled by them. This lasted so long that from words one finally came to weapons, our Cingalese declaring, and even our old good counselor Dom Joan (though not being a soldier) that never had Cingalese fought with so little fear for their lives. But being beaten back and, as far as ours were strong there, finding no provisions, they took the resolution to withdraw. Under the governor's orders, the enemy followed them and encamped above ours on the other side of the river at a place called Inda Hinacorle, called Owijttegammer, and another on this side of the river at a place called Poackpitte, where they were driven off by ours a few days ago, and the others followed them to the ruined Ruanelle, so that we now hear of no enemy anymore. The cities of Galle and Colombo we have forced and held with weapons at Ragia's request, but now we are requested to withdraw from these cities into his highlands for the security of his life, which we cannot do without also first securing ourselves well, and therefore we would have gladly seen that Your Excellencies from Batavia had been pleased to grant us a good fortification of sod in the Fatherland manner around a fine flat place on this side of Arandore and not more than an hour and a half's journey above Ruanelle to construct, which fortification then being provided with light artillery and further provisioned with everything necessary for a year, and provided with the lieutenant of the fort (which is a captain-lieutenant in quality), a lieutenant, ensign, constable, and 150 to 200 common soldiers, we would never have had to fear, and it would also be a certain means to keep the natives forever in peace and in our devotion. This same fortification would also serve as a market place for the Company, where its members could sell salt and other goods and receive areca in return, which would be brought by vessels to Colombo. The lands below down to Colombo would thereby be in eternal peace, and the farmers who have now abandoned their sowing for these marauders as well as their buffalo would be more encouraged to continue farming. Our highland provisions, consisting of more than 350 to 400 loads of rice, saved with great frugality and laid up at Arandore and Saffragam, we would then not have lost as food for the enemy. All these reasons have therefore compelled us, in God's name, to construct a good fortification with 4 to 5 points of sod.

Since the soldiers and sailors are inclined to drinking, and from the native arrack and sugar beer they sometimes drink themselves to death, we would nevertheless wish that your Excellency would remember us from the fatherland with three or four hired sworn midwives, since many—indeed (God willing:) most—young Dutch women bearing children are robbed of their health, and sometimes of their lives, by the bad practices and conduct of these native midwives. Three or four good apothecaries would also find work here. text_translated_detailed: Our lascarins from Matara, Colombo, Galle, and Negombo have been much sought after for several years now. Indeed, our own old adigaer from Matara, together with the dissava de Graeuwe, had the entire past season, along with other qualified heads of the Cingalese and all their lascarins, numbering well up to 600 in total, been at Batticalo. Such willingness the Portuguese never had from them, for without the help of our faithful lascarins from this south and west side of the island, it would have been absolutely impossible for us to secure our people so far from the coast, as now happens at Kotjaer, Batticalo, Calpatijn, and so forth. Since we observe and must acknowledge that our armies in the field cannot do without the help of these island warriors, and also that 100 of these are sufficient not only to drive away but to destroy 1,000 of the Jaffanapatnam men (who are cowardly, sluggish, and weak, unfit people), and when joined with our own people, are also capable of openly running to the assault against all enemies, as they have done before Colombo, Jaffanapatnam, and especially before Cochin. So we must handle this people somewhat gently and assign them leaders who are agreeable to them and who know how to govern them according to their customs, in order to oblige them somewhat more to us. We have granted all the Maturese and Galle lascarins who undertook the last campaign to Batticalo and Kotjaer all their lands freedom from jurisdiction, which is indeed very little for the Company but much for them. And it has pleased them so much that they only requested two months' time to rest with their wives and children, and then were ready to stake their lives in Your Excellency's service wherever it might be necessary. The complaints that came to Your Excellency there regarding the Malabar and Galle soldier pay books, we must acknowledge, were in many points not unfounded. But we must, to our sorrow and regret, repeat to Your Excellency again and answer on this point that we are still not provided with such competent bookkeepers everywhere, or it is impossible for us to prevent all abuses. In case Your Excellency were shown some books, both of the trade and of the pay, Your Excellency would be astonished at the great carelessness, negligence, sluggishness, and not a little evidence of the incapacity of some whom we must nevertheless employ for the books. And had we not found a competent merchant here to use in place of the merchant Montenack, we would certainly have fallen into confusion at Jaffanapatnam. Now, through the capacity of the aforementioned Montenack, everything has still come right, and the books came to us on the first of this month. We have sent as pay bookkeeper there the bookkeeper Gerrit Sijmon van Alpen, who has been reported to us to be capable for that position. In our previous letter, Your Excellency saw that we had to change the merchant Van der Duijn on account of his incapacity, and we had to do without one of our most capable merchants from the administration at Colombo. His position was again supplied by the under-merchant Arnould Sweers, whom we find capable and fit for that service. These aforementioned Sweers and Montenack are persons who learned the trade themselves in the fatherland, and we would still know of 5 or 6 more to employ. Nevertheless, regarding the pay books as well as the trade books, to maintain good order, we have placed these same bookkeepers under the supervision of the merchant who is placed over the administration, just as now at Jaffanapatnam the pay bookkeeper also stands under the aforementioned Montenack, at Galle under the merchant Blommert, at Colombo under the first administrator Van Vorsten, at Tuticorin under the merchant De Heijde. Whereby we hope that Your Excellency will be better served, and we will have somewhat more peace of mind. Your Excellency will please hold our deficiency in favorable remembrance and freely send us 6 or 8 capable under-merchants who are experienced in trade, and who are good writers, bookkeepers, calculators, and especially vigilant and conscientious men. For we shall know well how to employ such for the trade at Madura, at Batticalo, Kotjaer, Trinquenemale, and Calpatijn (which are all places of trade to be established). The Jaffanapatnam pay books have only come to us singly. We must now necessarily have them copied and send a set to Batavia, since they must necessarily be there for the distribution of monthly wages. Please assure Your Excellency that nothing is done outside Your Excellency's order under this government, and that no one enjoys more than Your Excellency's commands can allow. text_translated_detailed: Good to you and your Excellency at Batavia, the matter entrusted. It is as we also see that your Excellency has been suspicious of the multitude of powers of attorney that have been requested of us to remit the earned wages on your closed accounts to the fatherland and to obtain payment thereof from your Excellency, and therefore we have not this time consented to anyone to transfer their accounts in that manner unless they were such persons whom we could trust and who had not sold them, and since there are very many here who are married to native women and also some unmarried who wish to retain their previously earned wages so that they might receive them, we therefore wish to be instructed by your Excellency whether the Company might not be able to pay off under good security such accounts that have not been settled in the fatherland, whereby the Company, deducting 8 percent and 3 guilders per rixdaler, reckoning no damage in our judgment (under your Excellency's correction) would do — but such payment being made to the married so that they might better support themselves here, such people would be helped in their household expenses, those burdened with wives and children. To the Esteemed High-Honorable Gentlemen, the Gentlemen Commissioners at the Meeting of the Seventeen Esteemed and Honorable, How Honorable, Wise, Foresighted, Generous, and Highly Esteemed Lords, His Highly Commanding Lords. Since Your Excellency's High Honorable has benevolently been pleased, upon my request dated the 4th of January 1669, to dispose at their High Honorable assembly to such an extent that I should be employed in place of Batavia in Colombo in the honorable Council of Justice as a permanent member, with a monthly salary of seventy guilders [modern equivalent: Dutch currency], provided that I remain bound for a period of five years, as has appeared to me from Your Excellency's High Honorable very esteemed letters dated the 24th of August 1669, so I have deemed it my duty to thank Your Excellency's High Honorable for this in the most humble manner and to accept that offer. Nevertheless (with the approval of Your Excellency's High Honorable), since His Excellency the High Governor General and Council of India have graciously been pleased, by their letter dated the 27th of September 1668, to send me upon my request an act of improvement for the sum of sixty-five guilders per month, but without obligation of time, I might also be excused by Your Excellency's High Honorable from the five-year bond, for which favor I shall find myself highly obliged to prompt compliance with Your Excellency's High Honorable high commands, as Your Excellency's Esteemed and Honorable, Wise, Foresighted, Generous, and Highly Esteemed Lords. Your Excellency's High Honorable in Colombo, the 27th of November, Anno 1670. Entirely obligated, faithful and willing Servant, Bontanier.

text_translated_detailed: Fatherland. To the Esteemed Gentlemen Directors of the Chartered Dutch East India Company at the Chamber Amsterdam. Esteemed, Honorable, Highly Respected, Manly, Wise, Foresighted, and Most Generous Lords, Highly Commanding Lords. Since the ship Home to Velsen, by which these general letters and papers of this government also go, the Lord Courant was fully loaded and seaworthy, in order to depart ahead to the Cape of Good Hope, so between the 3rd and 4th of the same date, such a vehement and unheard-of weather storm arose as has not been much seen in the memory of men here, and by which we were not a little fearful for the ships Velsen, Cattenburg, and Soetendal which lay anchored in this bay, but—thank God—they remained preserved without considerable damage. The yacht Amerongen, which had sailed to the galleys eight miles east of this city in order to take on three elephants and about seventy loads of arrack there, to send the same to Colombo and from there to other places, was by the aforementioned storm, lying on a good anchorage between the 3rd and 4th of this month, torn from its anchors, so that one cannot yet learn where the aforementioned yacht has remained, or how it is, since it was a dark and narrow night and could not see far, whether the same has been lost with or without mast. text_translated_detailed: We hope that God the Lord will have preserved the aforementioned yacht, and that it will soon come forth again. And since the weather has now, thank God, calmed down again, the aforementioned ship departs from here for home to Velsen today under the orders of the Lord Governor Rijckloff van Goens, heading from this bay toward the Cape of Good Hope [Cabo de Boa Esperance], having been loaded in the aforementioned chamber according to your Honors' orders with such goods as your Honors will be pleased to review from the accompanying invoice and bill of lading, amounting to ƒ 411,240: 16: 5 [Dutch guilders, shillings, and pence]. God the Lord is beseeched to grant this costly vessel and the others that are to follow a swift and safe passage to your Honors. And we hope that the fluyt ships Soetend and Cattenburgh, the first for your Honors' chamber and the other for Zeeland, will be able to follow within twelve to fourteen days. The principal wait is for the Malabar pepper, which we are expecting and looking out for at all hours with the yacht Buijcksloot and the hooker De Swemmer. Joan Silvestre, here in the Company's service, has counted out two hundred and sixty rixdollars [Rijcxdaalders] in specie, which we request your Honors to be pleased to reimburse to the aforementioned person who is returning home with this ship Thuijs te Velsen according to the bill of exchange granted to him, with the respectful request to your Honors that he be honored with prompt payment. And since your Honors will come to understand the state of this government and consequently of this command in detail from our letter numbered 1: Cargo, we shall most respectfully refer to that. With which we commend your Honors, after our respectful greetings, to the holy protection of God Almighty, and remain. — Noble, Esteemed, highly respected, valiant, — and fortified, wise, prudent, and most generous Lords — and city. This 6th of December in the year 1670. Your Honors' faithful,

text_translated_detailed: Batavia to the Noble Lord Governor General Joan Maatsuijcker [Jan Maetsuycker], and the Noble Lords of the Council of India. Noble, esteemed, wise, esteemed, valiant, prudent, and most discreet Lords. It requested to be allowed to lay over in this river, which we could not refuse it. text_translated_detailed: It has also come to our knowledge that the eldest prince, together with several great men of the land, had attempted to wrest the conduct of affairs from his hands, seeing that it was leading to certain ruin and general damage which they foresaw would necessarily follow from his conduct. The King therefore had him guarded so closely and strictly by his watch that no one could see or speak to him without his permission, pursuing with great threats all those whom he suspected of having conspired against him. From this one can measure the confusion of that governance, unless one might believe that such rumors were spread in order to be able to use them in case of need, should they come to work against the Company over the breaking of the contract and seek some satisfaction. text_translated_detailed: thought it proper to seek help from that direction by presenting to them the injustice which he had suffered from a people come from distant lands under the guise of friendship, who sought to make themselves masters not only of him but of all of Malabar, that they had treacherously attacked him, murdered his wife and children, burned the land, desecrated the temples, killed the priests, robbed and broken the idols, dishonored the sacred, and done everything that fury could devise, so that not only he but all the Princes with whom he was allied, and consequently together ought to be set in motion to drive that people from the lands, since he was not only powerless but himself too weak to resist them, that they should provide for this in good time, so that it would not be too late, and he being brought under, they would find in him both their enemy and their lord at the same time, that he made this known to them in great need, and sought their assistance. He had written thus to the Raja of Cochin [Kochi:] that they were indeed enemies according to the laws of the land, but that they had never yet broken out into such great wickedness, nor into such irreconcilability that no peace could be made without needing the help of a people that would bring both the one and the other under subjection; the truth of these letters was received according to the disposition of the minds to whom they were sent, of which the greater part knew otherwise and therefore the deception was quickly discovered. Yet he did not cease to put his plans into effect, in order through the same to restore somewhat of his own and his [ally's] position, to which end a good force was gathered, stationed at Cranganore [Cranganoor:] with the threat to make a storm, but seeing that place well manned with people, after some skirmishing they withdrew again to their stronghold, where they then threatened to attack the fortresses of Cochin, and found no advantage either since those were well provisioned and the King with the Prince were present there. However, after the departure of the Ceylonese militia, they were warned by a Dutch deserter how the fortress of Cranganore had but few sick soldiers in garrison, and notably in two outer guards, whereupon he then set his eye on it with about 700 to 800 men and on the 5th of June at midday made an attack, but were forced to withdraw by the brave resistance with the loss of one dead and 9 wounded, after which, finding luck nowhere, they finally began to speak of negotiations for peace, to which end they sent hither such a letter as is translated here below, along with our answer and also the conversation which the Honorable Captain Burghart had at Cranganore with two of the foremost council lords. At this beginning we also received knowledge that already on the way from Tuticorin [Tutucorijn:] toward here from Ceylon 200 soldiers had come to Tengepatnam [Tengapatnam:] and we feared that the rumor would again bring some hindrance to the progress of the hoped-for peace or at least give occasion for the enemy to arm themselves anew. Seeing thus that unexpectedly from the land of Ceylon toward here came a force led against him according to the running rumors, we had them held at Cochin [Coijlan:] until we would see where their intention was directed, receiving from there the second answer as it goes here below, but because we noted that these letters came from persons who in no way could bind the state of the Samorin [Samorijn:] and could commit to what we had agreed with them, which was now however clear enough, for nowhere appeared the Samorin or the highest government to have given them order and command, it seemed to us that these letters concealed some deception, in which we were further confirmed by a timely [report] how the enemy on one night at the fortress of Bodenjadecoddy [Bodenjadecoddij:] had laid out a new [fortification], and gathered people in a place from where they could do great damage to the land, making that pagger [pagger: a fortified position] fast with great diligence, our men having sought through some skirmishing to drive them from there and to prevent the work, but it was not possible since the King's people after one dead and 6 wounded had been driven back, being forced by another heavy guard to secure the land. Before this news came over, we had sent an answer on the 16th of July, as the copy shows, establishing that their meaning did not accord with their words and came over

And since it has been generally believed that the transport of pepper by land was entirely within the power of the Raja, if his Highness wished to oppose it, by watching the passes and rivers, so we also understood that the same would have to be paid by the Honored Company for the account of his Highness, being as we were then still not assured of the faithfulness of the overseers who would be placed over it. And since the Raja has many times shown his inability through the disobedience of his own subjects, together with a request for the Company's help, so it did not seem to us better than to take the matter into our own hands ourselves, which we undertook immediately, placing various guards of Christian and native servants, and with these we have already fairly much hindered and blocked the pepper export and seized it. This work is of so much greater importance because we now have at court a man who can drive such matters forward in all ways and pursue them further. The Thieves' Island we had proposed in our letter to the fatherland to secure with a permanent guard, to which we were urged by Cochin and Teckencour, because the pirates held themselves in that vicinity, from where they plundered the entire land of Cochin and made the rivers unsafe. Thus, without good convoy, we dared not trust anyone by river to Porca, Calicoilan, and Coijlan, where merchandise had to be sent too many times. These robberies were so much more dangerous because we perceived that the same were helped and encouraged by the Porkatter, and that various great persons were firmly attached to this, who, finding their advantage in it, harbored the thieves and allowed stolen goods to be sold openly in their territory. When spoken to about this, they gave such an answer that one could not understand it otherwise than that they considered it good, for when Porca was shown the persons and robbed goods of the Company's subjects and justice was requested for it, it gave as answer that, since the Raja of Cochin could not prevent such things in his kingdom, it was also not obliged to detain those people in its territory. Now we wanted to seize the opportunity that the Bettetsen Coijl or Godormo had settled near that place in the territory of Berckencour, from where we sought to drive him away with some vessels, as has also been mentioned before. Under the pretext of blocking the entrance to the kingdom by occupying the Island against that open enemy, but we found that Teckencour had held back, and Berckencour openly showed his displeasure in favor of Porca, who also complained greatly about this. Therefore, we had to postpone our intention at that time until a better time, so that besides the Samorin and Godormo, we would not provoke more feigned friends into open enemies. Finding, however, a very suitable place on the mainland of Cochin, where we have led a guard of Dutchmen and natives, keeping that river and sea clean and free of robbers, with which everything has remained safe until now. To this, no small help was the fact that in the recent expedition the Honored Captain had seized one of the robbers' vessels, whose occupants, taking to land, fled into the city of Cochin and into the forests, and two of them were caught alive, where they were impaled by the King's people at that place, besides another whom they had killed in the pursuit.

To this we could not easily bring it, since trade had for a time been fixed with one merchant with obligation and pledge, which manner of trading promised much good if one could find such great and capable merchants here who were suitable to get all the pepper into their hands through their own conduct and practice and could answer for such considerable capitals as one would have to trust them with. However, such persons are not known on the whole Malabar coast until now, but rather some small merchants or Canarijns [local merchants] who do not possess such means, therefore could not bear the name of capable ones, nor can they get pepper into their hands except through force and the condition that the Honored Company could only buy the same from them and from no one else. For, as regards their means, we find that they must trade the merchandise of the Honored Company before they have the power to obtain pepper, which, if the same were given to them on credit for a time, they would thus pay us with the profits, the Honored Company running the risk that those debtors will become insolvent, as has happened many times already. The Franciscan friar Joan des Angios has up to now made no further request to depart, nor given any other signs than that he wishes to remain in the papal faith, without pursuing the hope that was expected of him. Whether it is that he now finds himself content in this church alone, or that he has been discouraged in his previous intention, or that he has made such a bargain with ours to be so much more agreeable, or whether he is hindered somewhere else—in any case, we find no reason to say anything else of this monk than that he continues in Roman errors. The Raja of Teckencoer [uncertain: possibly Tikkur or similar] had at the beginning of this year shown an intention to come personally to Cochin in a few days, but this did not follow, and was possibly held back by the preparations for war against the Samorin [Zamorin], as well seeing that the Honorable Company would wish to make no other peace with him than that which would be advantageous to Your Honors and the Raja of Cochin, and such could not possibly be granted by the Samorin (through means of negotiation), seeing therefore much more war than peace ahead. Otherwise we cannot see it otherwise than that he remains well-disposed toward the Honorable Company, showing this principally toward the Dutch children and the preceptor Hasencamp lying in his land, to whom his Highness shows much favor, having arranged with the greatest Brahmins of the land that they should instruct them thoroughly in the Malabar language, being now busy beginning the chief language called Sanskrit, in which all matters of importance are discussed, intending to send some more children there; however, with the teaching of the Latin language among the children of the indigenous Thomas Christians it does not seem to be proceeding.

text_translated_detailed: Comptoir Canara on the 3rd of July, anno 1670. On the 3rd of the same, the resident De Bruijn and bookkeeper Siewert Baecker go to the head merchant Narnamaloe to come to an even state of reckoning at his Esteemed Lordship's dwelling, where we first negotiated over the price of the two elephants named Orive Vellia and Vamadia, when we finally agreed for the two said elephants 2800 Rixdollars, namely for — is 1 elephant named Orive Vellia of 5 cubits [modern equivalent: approximately 7.5 feet] high, the other named Vamadia of 4 cubits and 11 inches high — 1300. 2 pieces of elephants reckoned at — Rixdollars 2800. After the agreement on the price, we proceeded with the said Narnamaloe to the reckoning of the rice transported, and having done this, it was found that the Esteemed Company's account exceeded the aforementioned elephants by 4871 Rixdollars, which remained as a debt to his Esteemed Lordship. Therefore we asked whether his Esteemed Lordship would accept the few merchant's goods that were in our warehouse in settlement of the aforementioned debt, whereupon Narnamaloe gave in answer that if we would give those at the price as previously sent to Cochin, he would gladly accept them, but because the Esteemed Mister Commander Hendrick van Reede has ordered us to deliver the goods for no less than the Surat price, whereupon Narnamaloe answered that he could not accept those at this present rainy season, but would accept the goods at an opportunity when he saw occasion for their sale, so that Narnamaloe in place of those merchant's goods requested his payment of 1720 Rixdollars. In the Comptoir Canara on the 3rd of July, anno 1670 in cash, and because his Esteemed Lordship showed himself unwilling to accept the goods at the Surat price, we have paid the aforementioned debt of Rixdollars in silver specie at his request.

Pulle accompanied him to outside the exit of his lodging, where His Excellency, mounting his horse, turned back together with him to the lodge. However, having ridden a short distance, Pulle came riding up at full gallop with several of the son of the lord and other persons of standing, along with their retinue, to escort His Excellency back to the lodge. But having come halfway, His Excellency thanked them for the honor and the trouble taken, requesting that, since it was late and the way was far, they would be willing to return to their lord. This they did at His Excellency's insistence. Thus continuing on our way, we arrived around the cook's time—half past eight o'clock—back at the lodge, where His Excellency found everything well and in good order. His Excellency then betook himself to the evening meal, as was customary, and retired to rest.

March 2nd, Sunday. In the morning, His Excellency had everything prepared and the soldiers stationed to go and fetch Pulle. When word came that he was already halfway there, His Excellency got back into the palanquin, proceeding with his company. A cannon shot was fired at two musket-shot distances from the lodge, passing by the Nayak's old fortifications, to meet Pulle. He was then saluted, and together they returned to the lodge. Upon alighting, His Excellency escorted Pulle inside under the salvo and discharge of cannon, standing at the entrance and then bringing him upward into a hall prepared and arranged for the meeting. Both went and sat at a table in the middle of that same hall. His Excellency seated that same Pulle at the head of the table, along with the chief merchant Pijl and other council members on chairs beside the table, just as Pulle's qualified attendants sat opposite. After some discourse back and forth, His Excellency proceeded to the actual matter.

text_translated_detailed: Standing at the entrance and then bringing him upward into a hall prepared and arranged for the meeting. Both went and sat at a table in the middle of that same hall. text_translated_detailed: These reasons appeared so agreeable to Pulle that one could clearly perceive his satisfaction. text_translated_detailed: Pulle declared upon this with full words that he acknowledged we had great reasons, promising to have everything restored according to our own wishes and that we could make such a dwelling as we desired, all with an appearance not only of earnestness but also of sincerity and uprightness, which was immediately seconded by His Excellency with equal good will, and that the Honored Company would henceforth extend their trade and commerce with greater desire and inclination than before, just as this happened along the entire coast of India, in Surat, Bengal, Persia, Coromandel, and so forth, where the Honored Company, being situated in very spacious and suitable dwellings and even in cities and castles for their greater security, were lodged. That all those lands, through our extended trade, flourished and prospered. That we had restored the king himself at Cochin, rather than appropriating his lands to ourselves, as was known to all the world. And that we moreover maintained that same king against the Zamorin. That the fortifications which the Honored Company had on Ceylon were built by express order of Raja Singa, whom we now also alone kept standing against his unwilling subjects, who would otherwise long since have been murdered, as was clearly known to him and all the world. That if the Honored Company had a good dwelling and firm residence at Tutucoryn, the Nayak's lands would also be better protected. That likewise it was known to all the world what security the Nayak had from Tanjore at Nagapatnam, where he would have found a safe retreat against the Moors two years ago. That the Company's intention was good and virtuous, not to wrong the Nayak, but to secure ourselves against scoundrels, thieves, and sea rovers. That we were now, as Pulle himself saw, unable to conduct any trade, much less to properly secure the Company's merchandise or to store their goods. And in case of misfortune from fire, all those goods would be destroyed. Item, the Honored Company required at least one thousand last [approximately 1,000 tons] of goods in warehouses, and that these, along with the necessary buildings for dwelling, should be built near fresh water, since the water in this dwelling being brackish would cause great sickness among our people. Pulle then responded with affirmative words, saying that having seen the Company's dwelling, he found it in no way suited to our condition. Therefore, the Honored Company was permitted to build a dwelling as large or as small, and in such form and manner as pleased them, with warehouses.

text_translated_detailed:
Extract from the letter by the Honorable Lord Admiral R. van Goens, dated the 7th of July 1670, written to the Honorable Lord Governor Anthony Pavilioen and the Council at Palliacatta.

We have regarded the request of the regent of Tegenapatnam as a matter entirely beyond our power, and it is the Company's necessary policy on this island. Moreover, all the fruits that Battacalo and Cotjaer produce, such as nelij [uncertain: possibly a type of wood or product], timber, wax, salt, cinnamon, and ebony, shall henceforth remain for the Honorable Company's own necessity. And since Raja Singa has ceded the aforementioned eastern harbors as well as Calpatijn to the Company by open deed under seal and with his signature, and has himself requested and qualified this possession, all foreign merchants shall make no distinction between these places and Colombo, Galle, and Negombo. Regarding Calpatijn, we are already so far advanced in the Company's trade that we hope in a short time to turn away all foreign merchants, to which the service of the Honorable Company and the peace of this island are most highly committed. We are now beginning to practice the Company's policy that all those who buy their cloth in Colombo and Galle are free on Calpatijn from all incoming duties, and then the Honorable Company has, in place of toll, no less than 60 to 75 percent profit on Coromandel cloth, and even more on Madras cloth and Tuticorin linen. And since the Company now certainly has sovereign jurisdiction not only on Ceylon, but also over the Madras harbors and the entire bay, we beseech Your Excellency, according to your ability, to support the Company's policies and to have them supported, so that henceforth every merchant in India may be brought to the custom and understanding that Ceylon shall be no more freely navigable than Batavia. We have good

Anno een duijsent seshondert en 'tseventigh den 30:e augusto, door de goede geheugenisse — die den sirumale chedu padi kata teuver — heeft van den heer admirael, zoo sijn tot â — present in gesontheijt, zonder eenige — verminderinge, ende laat ons schrijven die uwe goede gesontheijt. In den tijt dat den heer naijque van Madure— tegen mij den oorlogh heeft aengevangen, soo hebben den Vanamgamuedi ende Vellanteruvan daer hem den chiniatambij mudalij oock bij voechde onse Landen berooft en veel quaats gedaan. Nae dat den hr. naijck van madure met mij vruntschap gemaeckt heeft, soo is den vanamgamuedij eenige daagen in mijnen dienst gebleven, onder wijlen beraetslaght, hebbende met den naijque van Jan zjaver is denselven derwarts heen wegh geloopen, welcken naijque van tanzjaver hem gelaste te verblijven in de fortresse van Mannarkoijl hem oock eenigh Volck tot sulp gevende met den Vellanteru van samen beraatslaagende om mijn Lant te beroven, en veel quaats daer in te doen gelijck zij Van amgamudeij e, Villanteruvan met haar volckeren in mijn Landen van patukote en meer andere Lantstreecken hebben gedaen, doende grootquaat en veel onhebbelijckheeden, aen 't volck van ons Leger, sonder respecte van ijemanden welcke tijdingen mij zijn doen weten. Om welcke reeden met mijn heele Leger van gramanada purao: ben uijtgetrocken en gecoomen nae patukote, daer heeft evenwel den vanargamusdij zulcx niet ontsien noch gevreest, 't geene wij doen ter weeten zijn gecoomen, van pattukote vertrocken zijn nae mannarkoijl Vanamgamuddij ons vertreck en aencomst gehoort hebbende, vluchte van de fortresse Mannarkoijl, in welcke fortresse noch verbleven andala annargal ende mutiapa mudali met ses hondert Lascorijns en 150„ paarden, waer op onse Lascorijns een storm deden, dootslaande 150„ â 200„ mensch en 50 â 60„

2a6 v. 12th October 1670. On Translation of an ola [a palm leaf document] by Jaffanap, received the same day sent.

In the year one thousand six hundred and seventy, on the 30th of August, by the good remembrance that the Sirumale Chedu Padi Kata Teuver has of the Lord Admiral, so they are at present in good health, without any diminishment, and let us write of your good health. In the time that the Lord Nayak of Madure began war against me, the Vanamgamuedi and Vellanteruvan, to whom the Chiniatambij Mudalij also joined himself, robbed our lands and did much harm. After the Lord Nayak of Madure made friendship with me, the Vanamgamuedi remained for some days in my service, during which time, having taken counsel with the Nayak of Jan Zjaver, he ran away to that place. The Nayak of Tanzjaver ordered him to remain in the fortress of Mannarkoijl, also giving him some people for support. With the Vellanteru, taking counsel together to rob my land and do much harm in it, just as the Vanamgamuedi, Villanteruvan with their peoples in my lands of Patukote and many other regions did, doing great harm and much mischief to the people of our army, without respect for anyone. These tidings were made known to me. For which reason, with my whole army from Gramanada Purao, I set out and came to Patukote. There, however, the Vanamgamusdij did not fear or dread what we did, knowing we had come. From Pattukote we departed to Mannarkoijl. The Vanamgamuddij, having heard of our departure and arrival, fled from the fortress Mannarkoijl, in which fortress there still remained Andala Annargal and Mutiapa Mudali with six hundred Lascorins [a type of soldier] and 150 horses. Upon this, our Lascorins made an assault, killing 150 to 200 men and 50 to 60

text_translated_detailed: In the Year of Our Lord 1670, on the 19th of August, we undersigned, both greater and lesser heads of the three dessaveschappen [administrative divisions], Calare, Sjampanture, and Accrepatte, falling under Batticaloa, declare that we have taken as our King and sovereign, just as we do take and acknowledge hereby, the well-esteemed general, Dutch chartered East India Company, and in its name, the Admiral and Governor of this island, and his council, whom we hereby promise henceforth, and so long as sun and moon shall shine, to remain faithful, true, and obedient, without on any account, however it might be, abandoning them, falling away, or placing ourselves under any other potentates or governments. We further promise to the said Company faithfully to bring and allow to be enjoyed all such rights as we were formerly obliged to bring to King Ragiasinga [Rajasinha II]. And we shall render to the said Company such services and faithfully execute them as were formerly laid upon us by Ragia Singa, and which we obediently fulfilled and executed. We further promise that we (except the paddy which we need for sowing the fields and the maintenance of the inhabitants, both for ourselves and for the necessary cultivation with cattle) shall deliver and cause to be delivered to the said Company all the paddy that shall be sown and harvested in the aforesaid three dessaveschappen, and that for a larijn [a monetary unit] per amme [a measure of grain], without our being able to retain anything thereof (except the necessary maintenance of the inhabitants and what is necessary for sowing the fields) or to sell, exchange, transport, or allow to be sold to other foreign nations. We further promise that from now on we shall provide to all Company servants at Batticaloa, Chinneca, Latbedellen, and likewise residing in these dessaveschappen, or who might come to reside therein

text_translated_detailed: In the Year of our Lord 1670, the 16th of September, we undersigned, both great and small heads of the territory of Coljaar [Koljaar], declare that we have taken as our King and sovereign, just as we take and acknowledge by this present the well-esteemed General Dutch chartered East India Company, and in their name, the Admiral and Governor of this Island, and his council, whom we hereby promise henceforth, and so long as sun and moon shall shine, to remain loyal, faithful, and obedient, without for any consideration, however it might be, to abandon them, to fall away, or to place ourselves under any other potentates or governments. promising moreover faithfully to the Honored Company to bring in and allow to be enjoyed all such rights as we were formerly obliged to bring in and deliver to King Ragia Singa, and that we shall perform and faithfully execute to the said Company such services as were laid upon us in former times by Ragia Singa, and which we obediently completed and executed, and this because we certainly know that Ragia Singa has transferred and granted the gates and lands of Batticaloa and Coljaar to the Honored Company by letter, we promise likewise that we shall deliver to the Honored Company, and cause to be delivered, all the rice that shall be sown and harvested in the territory of Coljaar, and that at the price of the land, regulated according to that of Tammelegamme [Tammelegamme: a place name], being somewhat less than four stuivers [stuivers: a Dutch coin] per parra [parra: a unit of measurement], without that we shall be able to retain anything thereof (except the necessary maintenance of the inhabitants, and that which is necessary for sowing the fields) or to sell, exchange, transport, or allow to be transported to other foreign nations. we promise further that we shall from now on to all Company's servants residing in the said territory, or who

text_translated_detailed: Whereas King Ragia Singa by express letter, has earnestly requested the Honored Company, and for assurance against his enemies has desired — not only to take the lands of Batticaloa, with all that depends thereon, but also the lands of Coljaar and others, expressed in the same letter into possession, so it is that we the same, after the interest and desire of the aforementioned Ragia, and especially for the assurance of the state of the Honored Company having accomplished, first on the great bastion at Killewitti [Killewitti: a place name] before us have appeared all the great and small heads of the territory of Coljaar, consisting of 44 heads, just as many as there are villages in the said territory, and — thereafter in the fortress Trinquenemale [Trinquenemale: a place name] — have sent their delegates, consisting of a number of 36 persons, which have earnestly requested of us that we, as — other subjects on this Island, would take under our protection, protect from all domestic and foreign violence, and furthermore — in the name of the Honored Company to rule over them as King and sovereign, just as they today, all by express written request have shown, which we then in the council of this Government further after the interest of the Honored Company having considered, so the request and desire of the aforesaid both great and small heads, has been granted to them, just as we the same grant by this present, promising to rule them in all fairness according to our laws, and to demand no more rights from them than is fair and reasonable, and they have been obliged to bring in and pay to King Ragia Singa, furthermore to free them from all violence and harassment, which might be inflicted upon them from within or without at any time, to the best of our ability. text_translated_detailed: Concept Memorandum for the Esteemed Commander Jorephaes vosch [uncertain: possibly a name] and Council at Jaffnapatnam [Jaffna]. Since the advices from Colombo do not permit me to remain here any longer, although it would be desirable for the service of the Esteemed Company that I could have spent some more time with you to put necessary order to various matters, particularly concerning the redress of the wannias [local rulers], the provision of churches and schools, and such other things as would be deemed necessary, yet since this is presently impossible, I have nevertheless thought it good to note the following in memorandum, so that in time and when certain points can be further meditated, deliberated, and concluded with you. We conduct ourselves toward you with respectful deference. Since then, with the approaching hot season that has begun, the merchants have started to depart, and the remaining Company merchandise cannot be sold, nor has anyone inquired after any of it. For this reason and cause, in our writing of the 16th of May we detailed to Your Esteemed Honor the sending of all of it to Basra, and we persisted in that intention, and on the 29th of May last past from Gousaratta under the escort of the under-merchant Georgius Hartsincq—having arrived at the roadstead of Gamron, the two native vessels which Director Bogaert had advised us of with certain goods, which we intended to send to Basra, after the freight goods that had been brought were unloaded. In them were shipped the remaining unsold merchandise, the following:

70,568 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 32 metric tons] of pepper of good weight, brought in April last, costing 7,841 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency of the period]. 5,598¼ pounds of old benjamin of little value, costing 4,278 rixdollars and 16 stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coin]. 6,200 picul [modern equivalent: approximately 360 kilograms per picul] of Japanese copper staff, brought in February last with the ship the Pauw, costing with the additional charges 15,608 rixdollars and 12 stuivers and 11 penningen [modern equivalent: smallest Dutch coin]. Bruijto Japanese camphor, consisting of 291 bales, costing 7,530 rixdollars, 7 stuivers, and 1 penning. For expenses on the ships fallen to 18 rixdollars, 18 stuivers, and 4 penningen. Together amounting to 35,277 rixdollars, 15 stuivers, and 2 penningen.

text_translated_detailed: Esteemed and Honorable and High-Commanding Lords, the director of this place, who on account of the great heat and foul stench is presently staying in the village Saduan, has written to us alongside the sending of the foregoing regulations, Your Excellency's Honors, with one from there, if you would be pleased to order it, so that thereupon we had no further consideration, as indeed we also signed it, which has been done, confirming ourselves with the contents, and likewise ordered that if in the company's affairs anything were to have occurred not mentioned in the aforementioned writing, Your Excellency's Honors should be given advice thereof, but having nothing beyond that, we can mention nothing further than only that the company's caravan arrived here on the 23rd of this month, and was compelled for two days by hard weather to stop the unloading, as the sea was raging violently and it was not possible to get the cargo dry alongside, but as soon as the weather became somewhat calmer, we did not fail to hasten the unloading at once, which was completed today, and the ship, which is sent along with this to Your Excellency's Honors, is now entirely ready to weigh anchor at the coming night with the land wind and proceed on the journey. Also with this vessel, freight on Wingurla [Vingurla] has been earned a sum of ƒ2329:—:—, which for the company still serves well as relief for the shortage caused by the aforementioned yacht here. May God the Lord be beseeched to guide that costly vessel, whereby &c. Under the signature: Esteemed High-Commanding Lords, Your Excellency's Honors' humble, obedient, and duty-bound servants, was signed Adolf Willings and Paulus Vaans. On the side: Surat Persia. In the Netherlands Company's factory Ramron on the [date]. August. text_translated_detailed: For Spanbroek and Velsen, having unloaded at Tuticorin, and Soetendael at Gale, these three ships visited all the harbors on the east side of the island of Ceylon, provisioned themselves there, and caused no small commotion, as well as at Tuticorin. Whereby, if we then yearly received a strong return ship from Batavia via Coromandel and the silk ship via Surat, or otherwise via Wingurla and Malabar, we could yearly send Your Honors four or five ships by the end of November, all with fresh cinnamon and the merchandise that otherwise passes Ceylon by to Batavia, arriving about a month later, as daily experience clearly shows. We do not doubt that Your Excellency will have learned from our most recent letter dated the 9th of January of this year of the arrival of the ship Outshoorn, the reasons why we had consigned four ships to the Amsterdam Chamber in the previous year; and also how, in order to meet the Amsterdam Chamber halfway with the most recent shipment, we have sent 42,800 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 19,400 kg] of cinnamon more in the Outshoorn than had been shipped in the Beemster for Amsterdam. Your Excellency now comes with the fluyt [a type of merchant ship] Kattenburg at two-fifths and the Amsterdam Chamber in Veesen and Soetendaal at three-fifths of the returns which we have presently been able to send to the fatherland. We hope Your Excellency will be satisfied in the future regarding both matters. The cash in the amount of ƒ 10,050 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders] sent in payment has reached us well, and we wish that we might have been able to credit the general account in favor of Your Excellency's Chamber for a larger sum, since cash here is scarce, as Your Excellency will be pleased to examine more closely in the general letter enclosed herewith. How the cargo from Soetendaal is being delivered is shown to Your Excellency by the accompanying inventory. The captain and bookkeeper have properly accounted for the cash and ship provisions given to them, and we have received nothing but complete satisfaction from the captain, who has therefore also willingly agreed to repatriate with the same ship, and we do not wish to fail to recommend his person to Your Excellency. We could well have exchanged him with the captain of the Kattenburg, but since the captain of the Kattenburg is an old, experienced seaman and the ship is expensively loaded, we have thought it best to let each ship keep its own captain, as Your Excellency's order also indicates. The other officers whom Your Excellency has been pleased to recommend to us we shall not fail to advance in due time according to merit, for here on Ceylon we generally lack capable people, whereby those who conduct themselves well easily come to advancement. The Mister van Doens thanks Your Excellency most highly for the goodwill shown and congratulations on his son's advancement, not doubting that Your Excellency will receive from him complete satisfaction and pleasure. The piece of Rhine wine and two barrels of distilled waters sent by Your Excellency for the provision of the Governor's table have been brought in good condition and the Rhine wine has been found to be extraordinarily good, so we cannot fail to express to Your Excellency our gratitude for your generous provision, and that we are all the more obliged to the true service of Your Excellency by those who have had their share of it. What procurations [legal powers of attorney] have presently been passed again with Your Excellency's servants with us, in order that their deserved and well-earned monthly wages might be received with Your Excellency's permission, is evident from the accompanying list and extracts from the same. A greater number have indeed come before us, but suspecting that they might have been sold, we have refused to pass the procuration. Bartholomeus Laurens, who according to Your Excellency's letter was to have come with his wife Theuntge Bartholomeus van Rosendaal as free people with the Soetendaal, has not come before us but, according to the captain's report, remained behind. With Your Excellency's good permission—

text_translated_detailed: Cape of Good Hope to the Mister Commandeur Pieter Hackius and the Council. Esteemed, Valiant, now wise, aforementioned, very discreet ones. Under date of the 30th of November last, we have written to Your Excellency with the ship the House at Velsen in such manner as the copy enclosed herewith dictates. Since then the ships Soetendaal and Kattenburg have also become ready, for whose escort this letter is directed. Secondly, we have requested Your Excellency in our aforementioned most recent letter to provide us generously with garden seeds, which we have now thought good to do again, and to specify to Your Excellency which seeds will do well here, namely: cauliflower, savoy and other yellow and white vegetables, red and white beets, white peas without and without shells, each separately, gray peas, black radishes and rammelas. The quantity cannot be too large. Cos lettuce, lettuce, chervil, very necessary, cucumbers, fatherland carrots, anise, celery, Spanish melons, Roman turnips, beans, other artichokes, asparagus, horse beans, buckwheat, the healthy barley, young olive trees, which do very well here. Likewise laurel trees, carnation flowers of all kinds of colors and other flowers, grapevine shoots of the best sort, rosemary, if it is possible, cuttings of trees that in the fatherland have not passed through hot water. Please do not send us parsley seed, since it grows here as abundantly as grass in the field, just as also porcelain and several other herbs not mentioned here. We then expect Your Excellency's good care in what will be possible to fulfill, particularly please provide us with beans and peas, each one vat [modern equivalent: approximately 40-50 liters] of seeds. The same and all other seeds will be willingly received here by the lovers with a profit of one to two percent; if the advance payment could be purchased, it is also highly necessary here to be able to do the planting of everything ourselves,

Our sentiment being that Velsen should depart with the first Batavian return ships from there, because it is costly laden, so in case the 2 following ones had not arrived there before the departure of the first return fleet, otherwise these 2 or 3 could go ahead in the Company's service, as the previous order of the gentlemen of the Seventeen also brings with it, unless Your Excellency had received other orders there from the Mister Governor General and Council of India or our principals; Your Excellency would oblige us greatly by sending — a quantity of very young olive trees in boxes well cared for, as a little tree of Your Excellency's received on Ceylon grows as well as grass will on the field. The laurel tree here also grows very well with this, but the rose trees do not grow well and give no roses, it being to be wished that Your Excellency could give us some instruction. The carnations from the Cape have been received neglected and gone out. Your Excellency would do us great friendship by sending some sort of all kinds and other flowers. Ceylon being a fertile ground, richly, cool, peas, radishes, — roots, red beets, and rapeseed would delight us. Lettuce, parsley, and similar things here as well as elsewhere growing and giving seed. Some grapevine shoots in the earth would also be very pleasant for us. You are hereby with the Councillor the undersigned Your Excellency.

text_translated_detailed: To the Esteemed Lords Directors of the General Chartered East India Company at the meeting of the 17th in Amsterdam. Esteemed and Highly Commanding Lords: We give to your Esteemed Lordships, with all due respect, to know that we, your most obedient and humble servants, the Dutch burghers of this city of Colombo, and in their name, Louis Dutramble, Captain; Adriaen Daeck, Lieutenant; and Angelo Pegelotti, Ensign, how we petitioners, after this city through God's grace has come to fall under your Esteemed Lordship's power, have sustained ourselves as free burghers with all honest means, trades and occupations, as well as agriculture and seafaring, in the hope that in time through many of our efforts according to an old and praiseworthy custom here, a good burgher community and colony might be established, just as to reach that end abundant means are to be found on this island, whenever they are but taken up with desire and zeal, being therein well the principal ones to reach the right goal, agriculture and seafaring, which your Esteemed Lordship's Register of the soldier books which from Ceylon to the homeland are sent. Our last writing to Your Excellencies we sent from here on the 14th of August last with the boat Cochien to Your Excellencies directly, and a copy with the galiot Velthoorn to the Noble Lord ordinary councilor and Governor Rijckloff van Goens, under the request that His Excellency would be pleased to forward the same to Your Excellencies at a good opportunity, which we now greatly doubt, since we subsequently understood that His Excellency had departed for Batticalo [modern equivalent: Batticaloa], and from Ceylon no vessels were standing to depart for Batavia except very late, always not so timely that the aforementioned copy could have reached Your Excellencies before the last shipment from Malacca, so that we place all our hope on the aforementioned boat Cochien to be strengthened by orders from Your Excellencies regarding our proposals and requests. The aforementioned writing of ours was already around the end of July ready to depart with the galiot Velthoorn or boat Cochiem to Gale, to proceed with the fluite Duijnvliet to Your Excellencies, but contrary wind did not permit us to get those small vessels out of the harbor until the 15th of August. Having previously sent from here our request for necessities on the 13th of July to Ceylon so that Your Excellencies would be informed in advance by the Noble Lord ordinary councilor and governor Rijckloff van Goens, as Your Excellencies will be pleased to see from the copy of that date, sent under the enclosures with the boat Cochin, waiting at that time still only for the outcome of the peace negotiations that the Samorin [uncertain: possibly a local ruler's title] had then begun, so that we could inform Your Excellencies of some certainty.

Yet since we have been deceived so many times from there, that writing gives us no other thought than that they are again busy, as one says, to lead us by the nose, and to make us change or postpone our intention. Nevertheless, we would wish that we could bring this war to an end through a good peace. Before this, we have informed Your Esteemed Excellency in our last letter of the differences that still stood open there, to which end the Raja of Cochin had been drawn to bring the same to an end. Yet after he had spent more than a month fruitlessly, he finally came back without having accomplished anything, the mediation seeming to have fallen into greater estrangement, and it was not possible to come to good understanding with Parou. This became even more apparent later when the Raja of Parou shortly thereafter let such fierce complaints be made to us that everything appeared as if it would break out into open war, since they declared it impossible for them to endure any longer the violence and unreasonableness of the Cochin Raja with such earnestness that we found ourselves somewhat embarrassed to keep the matter in hand. The work of the princess of Attingal has borne no fruit, undoubtedly because someone is in our way there, which we shall for now still have to let rest, so as not to make her believe we are too much concerned with it. Yet we are assured by the promises of Her Highness that no Europeans shall be admitted. The trade along this coast stands still as we have previously reported to Your Honored [authority], now waiting every hour for a ship from Colombo for the pepper [shipment] to the Fatherland. This [letter] comes to Your Honored [authority] over [the waters], with the yacht Amerongen, which appeared here on the roadstead yesterday around midday from Persia, which has brought us from there the remainder of our requisition, as well as from Wingurla, 9,800 pagodas [modern equivalent: a monetary unit], which we shall still have ample need of for the payment of the Canara rice, amounting to 1,400 lasts [modern equivalent: approximately 2,800 metric tons], at 21 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: a monetary unit] each. However, the Honored [official] gave us hope that after receiving the cargo, we shall still be able to send more, about which we shall confer further with His Honor, following Your Honored [authority's] order. Now we proceed to our garrison books, together with an extract of our business accounts for the general office, up to the 28th of this [month]. To Cornelis van Woensel, proxy merchant, a bill of exchange has been granted here, according to the receipt of the cashier Gerrit Pruijstingh, amounting to one hundred Rixdollars at 60 stuivers [modern equivalent: a monetary unit] each, to be paid from the Company's cash box in Batavia to the chief merchant Joan de Vogel or the Honored Poolman. We assure Your Honored [authority] most respectfully. Your Honored [authority] is pleased to have the payment made at the warehouse, the general amount being ƒ 300:- properly credited here. In the Company's cash box, a sum of six hundred sixteen Rixdollars has been counted here by the garrison book keeper and curator ad lites [legal curator], for the account of the salary of Salomon Huwaert of Vlissingen in his lifetime, a ship's mate, which he made by testament on the 7th of January of this year, to the poor of Batavia, for which sum the general, being credited, we respectfully request that the same may be paid out there. With which we end, and remain, according to our humble petition, at your service. Your Honored [authority's] obedient and obedient servants. Was signed: H. V. Rheede at Draakenstein, Gelmer Vosburgh, Cornelis van Woensel, M. Boevius, G. Pruijstingh, and Frederick Houtman, secretary. On the side stood: Cochin.

text_translated_detailed: These same persons have falsely informed Your Majesty that we departed toward Batticaloa, and that we would ruin and destroy everything there, which has also been taken up by the great men of Your Majesty's court, who do not mean well toward Your Majesty, in such a way that they have turned against Your Majesty's inclination. This is clearly evident and confirmed when they have openly cried out before all the world that they had come to take revenge for the villages and lands that I had laid waste at Batticaloa and had slain the people, which is nothing but an open lie, and the contrary is known to all the inhabitants of this island. By doing this action, these wicked people make it clear that they employ everything to turn us against Your Majesty for their own profit, so that through this means they might have the opportunity to betray Your Majesty, as became apparent shortly after their departure to the lands of Colombo. We therefore eagerly await Your Majesty's answer, with great longing, because of the great love that we bear toward Your Majesty's welfare and the restoration of peace and quiet in His Majesty's lands. God preserve Your Majesty for many years. Remaining Your Majesty's humble and faithful servant in Your Majesty's castle, signed Colombo, the 24th of September. Rijckloff van Goens. text_translated_detailed: There appeared before me, Cornelis vander Hans, secretary to the visitation of the Honorable Rijckhoff van Goens, ordinary councilor of India, admiral and governor of the Island of Ceylon, the coast of Malabar, Madure, and so forth, in the presence of the undersigned witnesses, Jacob Schaepmeester, soldier in the service of the Honorable Company, who arrived on the 19th of July with the corpse of the ensign Hendrick Draeck, from Diteligke, where Raja Singa holds his court, and declared, with true words in place of an oath, that which is true and truthful: that three weeks before his departure from Diteligke, by attestation of someone who was very close to Raja Singa personally, and whom he had seen many times before and spoken with familiarly, Raja's face was swollen in appearance, his beard was white, and his eyes were thick, red, and protruding. He had a sickness in both his legs, which the deponent believes to be podagra or gout, and moreover his protruding pustules and swollen parts showed that he was severely afflicted with rupture, and also had other terrible sicknesses in those tender parts and elsewhere. He further declared that he had witnessed such horrible and severe murders, which without exaggeration (that such cruelty is found among the human race) cannot be heard of, and this happened most every day. That to offer to the devil, young boys continuously from seven to ten years of age were gathered in the land for this purpose and kept in the court, who then, when Raja lay in the pain of his sickness, five or six, sometimes ten or twelve of these innocent children were brought forth during the day and taken to the bank of a river, where first their arms were hacked off at the shoulder and their legs above the knee, and then the bodies were laid in small wicker baskets and surrounded with torches.

text_translated_detailed: We undersigned Sijwert Roos — ship's captain, and Reijnier Claessen second thereof and chief steersman in the service of the united chartered East India Company, stationed on the ship (that God preserve) named the House at Velsen, declare upon the inquiries and command of the Esteemed Lord Adriaen Roothaes, ship's captain of this city and lands, that the aforementioned vessel (presently anchored in this bay, fully loaded and ready to sail, in order to sail toward the fatherland) is sound, good, strong, and suitable, well manned with anchors, ropes, sails, and rigging well provided, and also well supplied with provisions as well as ammunition of war, as is proper, in order to undertake the voyage toward the fatherland, and to complete it with God's grace. Wherefore by these means we also declare — to be unable to allege any reasons, nor to know of any difficulty that could be made known. See why the voyage toward the fatherland with the aforementioned yacht could not be undertaken, presenting the same if needed and being requested thereto, we strengthen this our declaration further. Thus done and — passed as well as signed in the city of Gale on the island of Ceylon — in December, anno 1670: was signed Sierwert Roos and Reijnier Claessen. — Collated, accords against his principal - Gale the 6th of December 1670: — Edmont van Sterrevelt, secretary

text_translated_detailed: Colombo to the Esteemed Lord Rijckloff van Esteemed Ernstfeste, honored Goens, ordinary councilor of the mighty, wise and foresighted India government: the government of Ceylon, most generous lord. Esteemed lord. With the ship the Hoft van Breda, the 22nd of May sailed from here in order to anchor under Tutucorijn, and there to await your Esteemed order, we have under the same date sent our latest writing to your Esteemed, which with safe passage we do not doubt shall be brought to your Esteemed, and we have thereupon attached a copy by these means, so it could serve should the original, as we hope, not have come to your Esteemed, conducting ourselves therein respectfully, since nothing further has occurred to touch upon, wherefore this serves principally as a guide for 5 pieces of horses, and furthermore such goods as were requested by your Esteemed in the preceding years and have since come from Spahan, which we have all shipped in the ship Ameron from here with the 223 cargos of silk for the Esteemed Company received this year toward Batavia, sent, whose superiors we have instructed to deliver over Wingurla and Malabar to Colombo and to bring the aforementioned goods to your Esteemed. We hope the aforementioned horses will suit your Esteemed: should they, three of the same were at the time well purchased by the Esteemed Lord Director Goske, but then still unable to be able to send them, the others have now just come from Spahan. We have not been able to obtain more of that kind in this time, we shall not cease to obtain as much thereof as your Esteemed shall be pleased to demand, and at the next opportunity to send it over. The cost of the same and what further was sent appears from the attached invoice together to amount to ƒ 2652:3: 3, for which we respectfully request your Esteemed to be pleased to discharge this direction as is proper. No cash

text_translated_detailed: To the Esteemed, Highly Honored gentlemen, the Esteemed gentlemen shareholders, commissioned from the respective Chambers at the assembly of seventeen, representing the general Dutch chartered East India Company, at Middelburg. Esteemed, highly honored, well-wishing generous and commanding gentlemen. My gentlemen, Since our last advice dated the 11th of August of this year, sent to your Esteemed Highness over the land route of Persia, which herewith goes in Copy, nine days thereafter from here to Batavia have been dispatched, the ships Vlaerdinge, Loosduijnen and Swarte Leeuw, with a cargo of saltpeter, silk, wheat, etc. amounting to ƒ 233,438.13 [Dutch guilders], and in return received the following vessels from Ceylon via Coromandel, namely Soetendaal and Ijsvogel on the 24th of September, Spanbrouck on the 7th, and the small vessel the Dolphijn on the 21st of this month from Ceylon to Chiancos and Areeck, likewise from Coromandel 50 ropies [modern equivalent: a unit of weight] and 31,072 pounds of ginger, together with goods ordered from Persia for this district in fruits, wines, rosewater, alcatifs [uncertain: type of fabric], gold and silver cloths, amounting together to ƒ 94,092.13.8, received likewise from Batavia the ships the yacht Batavia, Gooijlant, Caneelboom, Witteleeuw, Hilvertum, and hooker the Vlieger, from there on the 21st and 29th of August, in company with the ships Durgerdam, Spreeuw, Blauwe Visscher and hooker the Molenaar toward here have sailed, likewise the aforementioned six vessels here on the 4th and 10th of this month have arrived, so that we with longing for the remaining four ships all hours await, may the Lord God protect them and bring them quickly to safety. Your Esteemed gentlemen in Batavia are only sending us silver, together with merchandise, gift goods and otherwise a sum of ƒ 150,868.9.13, and of which most of the merchandise is still on the ships Durgerdam and Spreeuw behind. The commanders of the various ships have reported that from below the line during 18 days and until near the Indian coast, very unfavorable

text_translated_detailed: your Excellency will find recounted that the situation for Sultan Maren against his lord father the Great Mogul appeared very favorable, as being the majesty in such a position to be able to hinder and preserve his posts around Agra, and which nevertheless will not be able to have any long duration, those troubles greatly incommoding the Company in Surat, with Agra lying well a capital of over 140 guilders [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] in return and cash ready to send, and to which the aforementioned resident saw little prospect, such that your Excellency will see that same arising from this return, and as the roads around Ahmedabad are also very unsafe, we fear that thereby the affairs of trade will encounter considerable inconvenience, may the Lord preserve the Company from damage. Always here in Bengal one knows of no difficulty, it being presumed that the Nabab Chaestachan is of the party of Sultan Masem, and which, being so, Bengal will remain wholly outside all commotion, unless the majesty in fleeing takes his course hither. The so-stitched blankets of which in our letter of the 8th of November 1669 over Ceylon mention was made, have not yet been delivered, having mostly arisen from the work which the Nabab Chaestachan has imposed upon the stitchers, such that they will only be able to follow with the next return fleet. Esteemed, noble, highly honored, very generous gentlemen, we shall conclude this letter, and your Excellency's high honors after our common respectful greeting commend to God's holy protection, and remain always Bengal at the Comptoir Ougly [Calcutta] the 10th of November, A. 1670. Your Excellency's high honors' obedient and faithful servants, Constantin Ranst, [titles/abbreviations], A. Weijns, Joan van Leent, Pieter Noortman, [titles], P. Hosmeester.
