Furthermore, the Comparant Gale Hamme Adigaer alone declares that after a considerable time, without being able to state the exact time, when the King Ragia Singa Rasu was in Nilobe, he ordered Tissobe (then Adigaer and Moetjaer of Matule), Carriapera Appohamij, Oeckoloewelle Mohandurem, and their lascars; also the Comparant Gale Gamme Matule Adigaer (being then still the chief of the lascars) with some lascars of Matule who are called Cattepoele, an Arache named Koeleheweij, and an arache of the lascars named Kattapoele to go to Lackgele; and that when they had come together there, on the order they had received from the King, they brought the Prince Commara Astana out of the house of the aforementioned principal major to a place nearby where the water for irrigating the fields is dammed up, called Rannamoere Ammoena, and that the Prince, standing near the edge of that dammed-up water, was pierced through by the aforementioned Koeleheweij Arache and Kattapoele Arache with their spears, so that he fell into the aforementioned water, and afterwards received several more stab wounds from many lascars.

Furthermore, the aforementioned Gopale Modliar declares in particular that when His Majesty Ragia Singa was informed of the death of the aforementioned Prince, he, the Comparant, was summoned by His Majesty, and that His Majesty then secretly ordered him to go to Lackgelle at the aforementioned tank [reservoir] and to see whether the aforementioned prince was also dead; that the Comparant thereupon came to Lackgelle and to the aforementioned tank when the aforementioned prince had been dead for three days, and also that he found the inhabitants of that village there keeping watch, whom he asked what they were doing there, and they told him that they were keeping watch over the dead body of Prince Comman Astana, which they also showed him.

text_translated_detailed: To the Honourable Gentlemen, Directors of the Dutch East India Company in Amsterdam. The Most Esteemed, Powerful, Wise and Prudent Gentlemen. — My Gentlemen, Being aware that Your Excellencies have greatly contributed to my promotion to Extraordinary Councillor of India, I find myself obliged to thank Your Excellencies most heartily for this, which I do hereby, with the promise from myself, through continuous good and faithful service, to make myself ever more worthy of Your Excellencies' favor. Having received notice of this my promotion in the month of March last, through a letter from the high government at Batavia, I accepted the same with respect and gratitude, as was fitting for me, but my salary was not improved thereby; whereas previously, namely on the 24th of July 1668, with the acceptance of the Governor's position, it had already been raised from 180 to 200 guilders per month, under a new contract of three years. And my promotion brings with it an obligation of 5 years, beginning when I should come to accept the same, which (as said) occurred last March. I hope it will be understood that (as it comes to that and I might write about it) the aforementioned 5-year contract should begin to run from the date of 24 July 1668, for I have not wished to make difficulties with the high government at Batavia regarding this matter, nor to criticize them, but rather to defer to the prudent judgment of the Gentlemen Seventeen in due time. The state of affairs here in Malacca, both regarding trade and other matters, is reasonable, the account books being closed as of July last with a clear profit, in 12 months' time, of 74,438 guilders, 11 stuivers, 1 penning [modern equivalent: approximately 74,438.55 guilders], as appears more clearly from the enclosed extract. That Malacca, which formerly used to fall so considerably behind, now passes, and can also in some measure serve as relief for the heavy expenses which Your Excellencies must bear everywhere in these lands for the maintenance and continuation of your state. The 300,000 pounds of tin or 800 bahars [modern equivalent: a unit of weight used in Southeast Asian trade] of 375 pounds each, which we are ordered to deliver to the fatherland, have already been sent in their entirety to Batavia, which I hope will be sold again with good profit. Whether now Coromandel, Bengal, Surat, and Persia will each be able to obtain their contingent is still uncertain, since tin ore comes to us at present somewhat scarce, being not always mined in equal quantities, as the seasons of the year, whether through too much rain or drought, or sickness and death among the workers, sometimes create obstacles. Moreover, liquor yields less and less tin, the Siamese making themselves masters of that trade. And the English have [text continues]

And the English have Queda in; they also came with a yacht and a small boat to Pera, from where they departed without accomplishing anything, their trade having been denied them by the King and the great ones there, by virtue of the contract which the Esteemed Company has with Aceh and Pera, which I myself made and concluded in the year 1659, for the maintenance of which I continually urged them through my letters, accompanied by pleasant gifts of little value. text_original: de voorgeroerde — ne pacquetten ons door opgemelte heer Baron heeft toegeschickt, daer toe te versoucken, om dat u Ed=e hooch Achtb: daar van geen mentie — elieven te maken, schijnende die pacquetten al eenigen tijt onder hem hebben berust, vermits schrijft uijt gebreck van ordre om een expresse daer mede aff te seijnden, geen andere gelegentheijt, dan 't vertreck van de heer Baron heeft gepresenteert, in welckers natie handen wij achten u Ed=en— hooch achtb: die ongaerne gelevert sien hebben bij 't affteijnden van dese, genomden Calckberner den ontfangh vande voorschreve pacquetten bedeijlt, ende met eenen versachdet, naar dat mochte toecomen, naar geen gelegentheijt te vertouven, maar met een expresse aff te teijnden, tsij over Batsara off oordellen veijlichst te wesen — „derwijle dat dese weijnich dagen is opgehouden, hebben aan den coopman Mierza zaptij vercost alle de aangebrachte candij suijcke zijn de man van 30 lb hollants, sijnde 4½ larijn meerder dan den lesten vercoop, waermede present besigh sijn den cooper toe ten ƒ 507287:6:10 Naar ons wert bericht, soude voorgenomden heer Baron van meeninge sijn met 't Engels particuliere schip Loijal Oxendent hier Int Nederlants Comptoir Gamron in Persia den 22en. April 1671. vooren aangeroert, naar souratta te navigeren, hem daerin seer verhaestende, apparent om dringende oorsake— waar mede d=le Hoogh Achtb: gebiedende Heeren— wij uEd=s hooch achtb: beveelen, inde bescherminge des alderhoogsten, wie u Ed: hoog achtb: persoonen in langdurige gesontheijt wil sparen, ende derselver voornemen voorspoeden twelck naar nedrige gebiedenisse sijn wenschende en biddende, die sijn ende verblijven — d=le Hoogh gebiedende Heeren Ed=le Hooch Achtb: onderdanige, Trouw, en dienst schuldige Dienaren Lulas Viender Loos Telling Duvel. 1 D: Lepelaar ƒ osects. text_translated_detailed: the aforementioned packets that have been sent to us by the aforementioned Lord Baron, we request that Your Excellency's High Honors would be pleased to make mention of them, as these packets appear to have rested with him for some time, since he writes that due to lack of proper order to send an express messenger with them, no other opportunity than the departure of the Lord Baron has presented itself, in whose hands we consider Your Excellency's High Honors would reluctantly have seen them delivered. Upon the sending of this letter, the named Calckberner has been assigned receipt of the aforementioned packets, and with one [instruction] to dispatch them, as circumstances might allow, without waiting for any opportunity, but to send them by express, whether over Basra or [to] judge [as] safest to be. Since this [matter] has been delayed for a few days, we have sold to the merchant Mierza Zaptij all the brought candy sugar at the rate of 30 pounds Holland, being 4½ larins more than the last sale, with which the cooper is presently occupied at ƒ 507287:6:10. According to what we are informed, the aforementioned Lord Baron would be of the intention to navigate with the English private ship Loyal Oxendent here at the Netherlands Comptoir [trading post] Gamron in Persia on the 22nd of April 1671, as mentioned before, toward Surat, hastening himself therein greatly, apparently for pressing reasons. Wherefore the High Honors commanding Gentlemen, we commend Your Excellency's High Honors to the protection of the Most High, who will preserve Your Excellency's High Honors' persons in lasting health, and prosper their intentions, which according to our humble obedience we are wishing and praying, who are and remain — the High commanding Gentlemen, Your Excellency's Noble High Honors, obedient, faithful, and duty-bound servants, Lulas Viender, Loos Telling, Duvel. 1 D: Lepelaar ƒ osects. Gu Cllinson

text_translated_detailed: 633739 Report of what the under-merchant George Wilmson accomplished in conducting the Company's merchant business within the city of Bassora [Basra], and furthermore what has transpired in the trade there, delivered to the Lord Lucas Vander Dusse, Director over the Company's important trade in the kingdom of Persia. Esteemed Lord. Since Your Esteemed Lordship has been pleased to send us with some of the Company's merchandise to Bassora, both to ascertain whether the same could be sold there at a higher price than here, as well as to inquire what further might be done and undertaken in the trade there, to which end Your Esteemed Lordship has been pleased to provide us with written instruction as regulation, and thereby to command that we conduct careful investigation and report on everything. Thus we shall according to the order of the same attend to everything that by virtue thereof has been accomplished & concerning the management and the trade undertaken. Upon our arrival there, which was on the 24th of the month of July past, I immediately endeavored to greet the Bassiak [Pasha] or Governor, so that by that opportunity I might ascertain what apparent possibility there might be to obtain for the Esteemed Company freedom from the — toll, whether in whole or in part. But since through his hindrance at that time I could not meet with him, but was put off, it happened through an accident to my leg that it was delayed some days longer than otherwise it would have been. Meanwhile, one of the subordinates was sent there, two days thereafter it occurred, and the toll freedom was requested, to which the Bassiak gave answer that the freedoms enjoyed in the time of Hossen Bassiak [Pasha] would still be obtained, and the Esteemed Company would be held in esteem above all Europeans. text_translated_detailed: Agra. Our resident, the first Bonde in Hindustan, and in Bijapur again negotiated some 300, and in the quarters of Goa over 800 bales of that blue dye, of which we apparently will only be able to receive a portion so early that it can proceed with the ships to Batavia this time. It has been very pleasant for us to perceive that Your Esteemed Lordship has been pleased to take satisfaction in the sale of the cargo brought last time with the court of Breda to Agra. Whatever cargo we receive from time to time hereafter, and at what reasonable prices they are sold, our successive dispatches will show, as Your Esteemed Lordship has demonstrated to us, upon which we hope to see no less satisfaction from Your Esteemed Lordship in due time; just as we have now also been very pleased to understand Your Esteemed Lordship's consent to be able to negotiate yearly, just as the English do as well, a quantity of tin, notwithstanding that it must be delivered to the King's factors. This obligatory delivery seems somewhat objectionable, but we have nonetheless had no difficulty with it thus far. text_original: verobeigechetij tijen, dat de voorseijde palles. tot welcke lage vercoop van de peper wij nooijt zouden getreden hebben bij aldien de fransen met een samelijcke quantiteijt, inde landen van razjur-baagh genegotieert, eens zoo groot van Correl als de mallabaarsche peper, gaande wegh voor 8½ abbassij vande hand— schooven, zonder dat ijmand naar d'onze omzagh, waa over in 'twel minen van VEd=le H: acht te raade zijn geworden met 5: a 600: man de hand te lichten, om te zien of de loop van hun daarmede gesluijt, en naar ons conde getrocken worden. dit soo drae niet in twerck gestelt of is gevolght gemelte quantiteijt voor 8: abbassijs afgehaalt, naderhand ½ abbassij hebben doen steijgeren, op welcke voet dagelijx bij parthijen besprooken, en uijtgelevert werde, zijnde tot nogh niet hooger te brengen geweest
text_translated_detailed: at such low prices for pepper, which we would never have agreed to if the French had not negotiated a similar quantity in the lands of Razjur-Baagh [uncertain: possibly Rajapur or similar region], of a grain size just as large as Malabar pepper, selling for 8½ abbassij [modern equivalent: Persian silver coins] per hand-measure, without anyone looking at ours. On account of this, it seemed good to the esteemed gentlemen to lighten the hand with 5 to 600 men, to see whether their supply could be closed off and drawn toward us. This was scarcely put into effect when the aforementioned quantity was purchased at 8 abbassij, and afterwards they caused it to rise by ½ abbassij, at which rate it was discussed daily in parcels and delivered, having not been able to bring it any higher up to now.

text_original: Patira Aan de Vergadering der Heeren, Seventhiene, representeerende de Indische Compe vergadert tot Middelburg in Zeelant en Transiaat uijt het persiaans— het Request der oprechte tweede persoon vande Hollanders. e oet ho inse e e al lan ee roa ate srot ole a a a ntui de eende geen ate o ebaene ae ooede oe ende t derbent weijn ender dach willende haar reijs vorderen, soo wierden ij overvallen bij eenen Alij sulthaan broeder van den emachten om Lenden en daegs inde stadt te gaan, gedroeghn goothomannen, neemt haar gevangen, ende voert haar in sijn plaats genaamt Boinacq, drie maanden naar het voorschreve voorval, drije andere hollanders passerende door denbent voornoemt, vernemende wat daar gepasseert was, hebben sulx den Gouverneur gecaagt, hem om hulx vragende, om de voornoemdens slaven ende haar goet weeder te becomen, verthoonende dat sij noijt gehoort hadden, datmen int Coninckrijck persien de passanten plundende & haar tot slaven maeckte den Gouverneur verwondert over dit nieuws, schrijft aanstonts aanden Chamkaal, hem vertoonende, dat door dese saack de reijsigers haar vrijigheijt benomen wiert, soomen soo wilde handelen, drong hem tot vrijstellingh der gevangenen, ende haar goederen, op dat sij mochten gaan waert haar goetdachte, al het antwoort vanden Champaal was, dat hij haar niet vrij soude laten dan door last des Coninx, den Gouverneur tot vertroostinge der hollanders, op dit antwoort, sent haar naar Chammagie de geselthagt met een megh mondaar om haar met noodige te versorgen, ende teijde gaat tot de poort des weenelts toevlcht, en presenteert request wegens t saack, — ende soo mij bevoolen wort u te helpen, sal mijn best doen, — ende alsoo dese persoonen in Spahan gecomen sijn, en ons het gepasseerde verhaalt, sijn wij schuldich geweest, om u dit doen bekent te maken, ende alsoo wij van tijt tot tijt hebben
text_translated_detailed: Petition to the Assembly of the Gentlemen, the Seventeen, representing the Dutch East India Company [expanded: Indische Compagnie], assembled at Middelburg in Zeeland, and Translation from the Persian—the Request of the second person in authority of the Hollanders. [uncertain: several words appear corrupted or illegible in the original] When they wished to continue their journey, they were suddenly attacked by an Ali Sultan, brother of the [uncertain: title or name], in order to go to Lenden and in the city by day, [uncertain: text unclear] Ottoman manner, he took them captive and brought them to his place named Boinacq [uncertain: place name]. Three months after the aforementioned incident, three other Hollanders passing through the aforementioned place, learning what had happened there, reported this to the Governor, asking him for help to recover the aforementioned slaves and their goods, showing that they had never heard that in the Kingdom of Persia travelers were plundered and made into slaves. The Governor, astonished at this news, wrote immediately to the Chamkaal [uncertain: official title], showing him that through this matter the travelers were deprived of their freedom, and if one were to act thus, he urged him to release the prisoners and their goods, so that they might go where they pleased. The entire answer from the Chamkaal was that he would not release them except by order of the King. The Governor, to comfort the Hollanders, upon this answer, sent them to Chammagie [uncertain: place name] with the company and a megh mondaar [uncertain: official or guide] to provide them with necessities, and at the same time goes to the gate of the [uncertain: title or place], and presents a request regarding the matter—and so if I am commanded to help you, I shall do my best—and since these persons have come to Spahan [Isfahan] and have told us what happened, we have been obliged to make this known to you, and since we have from time to time received courtesies from this gate which seems like heaven, we hope for the continuation thereof, so that we request that such [uncertain: text corrupted] be arranged, that the aforementioned prisoners and goods may be set free, to increase the fame of your justice, and that the aforementioned prisoners together with [uncertain: text corrupted] for your property to the end of their days, and we shall likewise without end under your protection remain obliged to your order in all things.

text_translated_detailed: patria duplicate to the Honored Gentlemen, Directors of the United Netherlandish East India Company chartered, at the assembly of Seventeen in Amsterdam. Honored Gentlemen, what had occurred was forwarded, which letters were sent along with the ships of their worth and the coaos boor specanide areto mal abboeden, and which we also hope will be received by Your Honored Gentlemen through a safe passage, there being still remaining for Your Honored Gentlemen's reason to Nienoordtwijck, placed by Your Honored Gentlemen at Batavia, to carry out the order for Thormanidel, which we intended to accomplish by the yacht the Pepper for the direction, and also ready. However, we understood unexpectedly that the aforementioned yacht the 3rd of February had the Coijlang water drawn, from there straight through the Maldive Islands undertook its journey to Persia, leaving the pepper for this year unable to be sent. Likewise, we intended to send our advices both for the direction and Your Honored Gentlemen, when yesterday there arrived here a private English ship, wishing to go to Persia, which good opportunity we observing, now obtained means to send this our letter to water in Persia, and from there by land to Your Honored Gentlemen and to forward. In our last by water we showed how we by our battery and heavy cannon had brought down the stone redoubt, and that we then expected the enemy would have come to reason for accord, or that we would have attempted to advance our works further. Which first turned out otherwise and against our hope, for instead of coming to terms with the Company, the same took up a posture of stronger resistance, to which he brought a very considerable force, which being positioned in such strong works, hindered our progress quite considerably.

text_translated_detailed: not one voyage was profitable, but all returned fruitlessly. — The Company's privateering vessels stationed at Queda captured a small ship or a Javanese gorab in the past February, which was the property of the King, the Company's enemy, but since the English said that the same vessel with its cargo was their own property, His Excellencies from Batavia sent the 5 elephants, the 778 marks of gold, and the 10,807 pounds of tin that were found therein, along with some other goods, back with the Company's ships—without orders to return these things, in case proof of English ownership was provided, to that nation again. Whereupon it followed that the Honorable Governor George Foxcroft at Madras [Madraspatnam] has shown us so much evidence that we have offered His Excellency to make the restitution if we were granted such a document concerning this as His Excellencies have indicated we must demand in that case, namely, that the same must be signed by His Excellency and His Excellency's Council of Fort Saint George [Fort S. George], and that the Company must thereby be secured or indemnified against all claims or further disputes regarding that small ship and its cargo, whether here in India or in Europe. text_translated_detailed: Copy. Surat, to the Esteemed Mr. Andries Bogaert, Director of the Esteemed Company's highly important trade and further management in the Kingdom of Guzerat and Hindustan. Esteemed and Honorable, etc. That we have received your Esteemed's letter of the 11th of June, together with the attached documents for Batavia, Malacca, and Palliacatte on the 7th of July, will have been made clear to your Esteemed by a small letter sent with the first cassettes. Since then, on the 18th, the duplicate documents dated the 18th of June arrived, which we have all forwarded to Masulipatnam after review, where they also arrived safely on the 17th of this month, and with the ship Rotterdam, which lay ready there for that purpose, were sent forward to Batavia, just as the letters for Malacca were also sent by that route. Since the Mayboom had already departed for Malacca on the first of June for the last shipment, it has been pleasing to us to understand that your Esteemed, through two good sales days and various merchants' goods at agreed prices specified thereby, had disposed of them, and consequently, with the closing of the account books in Surat, had achieved a clear profit of ƒ689,178:5:15, which in these difficult times is truly most gratifying. May the Almighty God graciously bless such upon the remaining and expected from Batavia merchants' goods more and more. We have since our last of the 28th of March further sold 19,414 pounds of Spiaulter [uncertain: type of spice or commodity], namely half coarse or unrefined, the rest fine or good mixed together at 14½ stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coins] per pound, 13,125 pounds of Lead, namely 10,525 pounds of those in Lengen at 4 1/16 stuivers per pound, 2,600 pounds of foul Pegus at 4/32 stuivers, 1,430 pounds of Quicksilver at 40 1/5 stuivers, 598½ pounds of Vermillion.

text_translated_detailed: Your Excellency: the directorate with respectful request that you be pleased to continue with our guidance. Concerning the sale of coarse English cloth in the East, the city is presently very small, since the neighboring pound has brought much of it and thereby everyone has been provided with it fully at 5 rupees per piece. Nevertheless, we have now for 4 or 5 days in succession been in conversation with the Company's cloth merchants, and as it appears, we shall obtain for the English sheared or gauze cloth of 1¼ ell at most 4½ rupees, and from the other cloths apparently little profit, the purple, crab-red, and dark colors being not drawn at all, and the crimson also little, though we shall give Your Excellency clearer advice hereafter regarding the actual outcome, which we had hoped to do now, and why these have thus been held up so long. These, together with some papers and letters from the Illustrious Governor-General Joan Maatsuijker and the Honorable Gentlemen Councillors of India, as well as from the Honorable Extraordinary and Governor of this Coast, Antonio Pavilioen, came to us on the 25th of this month, whose matter Your Excellency has already understood for the most part from the homeland documents, with which W. C. Hartsink and f. 3 were signed. Nijendaal, on the East side stood N. Comptoir, July in the year 1671. Golconda on the last day. Below also stood, collated, agrees. Masulipatnam, the 27th of August 1671, was signed Johannes Kruijf, First Clerk, accord after collation made. Money: 10th, 7th, 1671.

text_translated_detailed: Regulation. To the under-merchants, Messrs. Bartholomeus van Rosendaal and Cornelis Mersman, departing as chief officers toward Serigang and the other Comptoirs of Java and Pegu subordinate thereto. And also this month to the under-merchants, Messrs. Leendert de Lange and Hendrik Fedders, presently conducting the Company's business in that Kingdom provisionally as chief ministers. Esteemed, pious, discreet Sirs. The ship the Maypole has arrived here again from Serigang over the Palicat southern Comptoirs on the 5th of May last, when the under-merchant Mr. Bartholomeus van Rosendaal handed over to us the Serigang letter of the 27th of March signed by the Messrs. Joris van Coulster, Hendrik Fedders, and Mr. Johannes Verkerk, and the Report of the Messrs. van Coulster and van Rosendaal set down in the manner of day-registers concerning the execution of their Commission in the inspection of the Comptoirs there in the land entrusted to them, together also with the attachments of both these writings, and besides that also a particular Report written by Mr. van Rosendaal alone concerning the matters of the aforesaid inspection, wherein he, as also commissioned, was not used with van Coulster, just as he has also besides that given oral account of this and that circumstance there in the land concerning the trade and further service of the Honorable Company. Upon all which writings and matters now by means of this is answered and thus more advised and ordered, with this ship the purse of Amsterdam, departing today from here over Masulipatnam toward Serigang as in the following is to be read. Going these same into the hands of the Messrs. van Rosendaal aforementioned and the under-merchant Cornelis Mersman, who therewith travel over as chief officers there, and therefore by all and each one of the further servants of the Honorable Company there upon their arrival and following stay shall be recognized, obeyed, and respected.

text_translated_detailed: And ordered, with this ship the purse of Amsterdam, departing today from here over Masulipatnam toward Serigang as in the following is to be read. Going these same into the hands of the Messrs. van Rosendaal aforementioned and the under-merchant Cornelis Mersman, who therewith travel over as chief officers there, and therefore by all and each one of the further servants of the Honorable Company there upon their arrival and following stay shall be recognized, obeyed, and respected, just as we expressly command this by means of this, upon the oath with which each one is obliged in faithful duty to the Honorable Company. Your Excellency is also by this ordered that the former chief officer aforesaid Mr. van Coulster, together with his family, without fail be sent over to us with this ship. Since this has also been found good in Council here by Resolution, it must happen promptly, because he, without new arrived suitable reasons, directly contrary to our previous orders, upon the departure of the Maypole, remained there still, and indeed has made transfer of the Company's Effects to the Comptoir Serigang and sufficient distance from his previously recommended supreme authority over the affairs in that Kingdom, so long as he would be there in the land, and this would not be recalled by us. Just as now happens by means of this in consequence of that arrested suspension of his Chief Merchant's quality, etc. The Under-merchant Mr. De Lange has been granted his request for departure, so that we shall also certainly expect him back there as soon as possible, even if he perhaps changed his mind thereafter. He shall then from his intention make transfer of his chief office and administration in Ava to the aforementioned under-merchant Mr. Fedders, who has been chosen for this by this Council, as he is entrusted, together with the under-merchant Mr. Samuel de Lafosse, presently the person there, with the proper management.

Ende is de E: fiscaal daar doe ook op gevolgt ende voorts op gebleven tot het ontlost is geweest, maar en hebben, buijten een casje met eenige geringe cleijnigheden, door den commandeur Pieter Hackius aan de caap de - bonne esperance bij een gesamelt, ende over= gesonden, niet anders gevonden, dan 16 bortjens goude en silvere galon, een stuk poildesoij van 59¼ ellen, ende een stuk van 42¼. onder de onder coopman baldé om te bestellen aan den burger abraham struijs, welk een en ander dan ook door sententie van den raadt van justitie geconfisqueert is geworden, het gem: opperhooft aan de caap de bonne Esperance sal uw: Ed=e van het voorz casje en sijn devoir aangewent. om uw Ed:e last de voorz saak aangaande te voldoen, van daar in't breede hebben geschreven. waar toe mij sal gedragen, maar de brief die sijn E: nevens hetselve casje herwaarts heeft gesonden was geaddresseert aan de generaal ende de raden van India, uijt welks lecture dan de Heeren Raden contschap hebbende gekregen van uw: Ed:e ordre de visite van het gem: schip aangaande, soo en heb ik niet wel connen na laten haar E: E:
text_translated_detailed: Esteemed Gentlemen. The letter of the 12th of December of the previous year sent by your Esteemed Honors to me concerning certain goods and valuables which your Esteemed Honors had been informed were sent out under the under-steersman chief with the ship the Foresight [De Voorsichtigheijt], I have received, and I have understood your Esteemed Honors' intention concerning this. And thereupon I also immediately gave orders to the Esteemed Fiscal Pieter Pauw to send the Esteemed with a party of brave servants to meet the same ship in order to ensure that in the Strait of Sunda, around Bantam or the islands, nothing from the same might be handed over, which he then also encountered on the Bantam side and there took possession. And the Esteemed Fiscal also followed thereupon and remained further until it had been unloaded, but we have found, besides a case with some trifling small items collected by the commander Pieter Hackius at the Cape of Good Hope and sent over, nothing other than 16 strips of gold and silver braid, a piece of silk fabric of 59¼ ells [modern equivalent: approximately 44 meters], and a piece of 42¼ [ells], under the under-merchant Baldé to be delivered to the burgher Abraham Struijs, which one and the other has then also been confiscated by sentence of the Council of Justice. The aforementioned chief at the Cape of Good Hope shall write to your Esteemed Honors in detail concerning the aforementioned case and his efforts expended to fulfill your Esteemed Honors' order concerning the aforementioned matter. To which I shall apply myself, but the letter which his Esteemed sent hither along with the same case was addressed to the Governor-General and the Councils of India, from the reading of which the Esteemed Gentlemen Councilors having received knowledge of your Esteemed Honors' order concerning the visitation of the aforementioned ship, I have not been able to refrain from writing to his Esteemed Honors.

And since we could sufficiently assure ourselves that, so long as His Excellency the fiscal with his servants would be on board, there was no fear to be had that anything whatsoever could be handed over without his knowledge, so we deemed it unnecessary to inform the skipper and further officers thereof, as your Excellency's order otherwise also brought, relying on the fact that your Excellency will not take this dispensation amiss. The letters in the aforementioned case sent from the Cape have been opened and read here by the appointed Council of Justice, but nothing was found to be prejudicial to the Company. With which then this shall close and your Excellency, according to my willing obedience, I commend to the almighty protection of the Lord, remaining, Noble Gentlemen, your Excellency's very obliged and humble servant, Joan Naetsuyker.

T zedert is hier op den 28. ' December passado, goet loff van uEd=le Camer over d' Cabo de bonne Esperance met sader een een gesont volck wel aengecomen, de fluijt Papenburgh, hebbende een spoedige reijse van 5. maenden en 22. dagen en geen dooden tussen wegen gehadt, mitsgaders 133. coppen in 't landt gebracht, wesende twee meer als het getal 't welck uijt het vaderlant heeft gevoert, die aende Caep door eenige verwisselinge daer op gecomen sin. wij hebben daermede wel ontfangen, uEd=e gans aengename particuliere missive vanden 28. ' Junij des verleden Iaers, en daer uijt met vreughde verstaen de goede gewenste tijdinge, dat de retour vlote van 15. schepen, in november en December a=o 1669 van hier vertrocken, volgens het advijs van d' h=r raet Ordinaris Mattheus vanden Bronck, tot in 't gesighte van hitlant en fair hiee behouden was gevaren, en dat noch De nieuiwe erde sal werden geob serveert int boecken goederen hebben de gesoe den letters tot de druckerije ontfangen placant aengenamer is, hebben de opperhoofden van papenburg ons weten teseggen, hoe voor haer depart noch hadden verstaen de meeste schepen van voorsz vlote al binnen de havens onser landen waren gearriveert, daer voor de goetheijt des heeren moet gedanckt zijn
text_translated_detailed: Papenburg addressed this to the Honored Gentlemen Bewinthebberen [Directors] of the Chamber Amsterdam, Honored, esteemed, wise, foresighted, and most discreet gentlemen. In our most recent private letter of the 16th of November last, Your Honors were informed of the departure of four return ships for the second shipment to the fatherland under the command of the Honored Pieter Coopman, and it was advised that two of these same ships, namely the Vrijheid and Zuidpolsbroeck, laden with a cargo valued at ƒ780,338:4:14 [Dutch guilders] for Your Honors' chamber, were projected, just as Your Honors will come to understand more fully from the aforementioned letter, which has been sent in duplicate, regarding which we have conducted ourselves accordingly. Since then, on the 28th of December last, with good fortune from Your Honors' Chamber over the Cape of Good Hope, the fluyt [type of ship] Papenburg arrived safely with healthy people, having made a speedy voyage of 5 months and 22 days and having had no deaths along the way, and moreover brought 133 men to the land, being two more than the number which it carried from the fatherland, which came about at the Cape through some exchange there. We have thereby received well Your Honors' most pleasant private letter of the 28th of June of the year past, and from it understood with joy the good and wished-for news that the return fleet of 15 ships, which departed from here in November and December of the year 1669, according to the advice of the Honored Councilor Ordinary Mattheus van den Bronck, had sailed safely into the sight of the homeland and fair weather, and that still the new earth shall be observed in the books. The goods have received the letters intended for the printing house. The placards [official notices] are more pleasant. The chief officers of Papenburg have made known to us how before their departure they had still understood that most ships of the aforementioned fleet had already arrived within the harbors of our lands, for which the goodness of the Lord must be thanked.

text_translated_detailed: Jan van Dalen: Extract from a letter sent by the esteemed Commandeur van Reede and the Council at Cochin to the esteemed gentlemen directors of the United East India Company, dated the 16th of February 1670. The esteemed gentleman Governor Rijckloff van Goens has sent us an extract of your Excellency's esteemed letter dated the 19th of April 1669, concerning a certain Jan van Dalen, who had been in the service of the esteemed Company as an under-merchant, and here at Cochin passed away, wherein we find that his relatives make some claim over the goods left behind, as appeared by inventory, where more money seemed to have come than had been credited to his account, leaving us, the said his Excellency, your Excellency's esteemed, to take care of that. We have therefore had two persons examine the inventory with the sale, and thereby found that various things did not agree, such as that difference, as now goes herewith, which was not of such great importance, as indeed the cash which was noted on the inventory, the same should have been handed over to the merchant's clerk Pieter Smith, according to receipt given to the curator adlites, but how now the money has been used, we cannot well write to your Excellency's esteemed, since no one of those persons is present here, yet it is heard here from all that the cash has been in the Company's cash box, as the said van Dalen, as head of the comptoir Calicoijlan ending, from there came sick to Cochin and also passed away, without having previously made transfer of the Company's effects running there, also a post remains, at that time in the books, which equally brings out the same species and amount as on the inventory.

text_translated_detailed: 8 NV IL3 dn 225. My Lord, We have been greatly astonished to understand from the advices that have come to us from the Cape from the ship the Foresight, that Your Excellency, without having any reason whatsoever or providing any justification, has removed from that same ship (under the pretext of inviting him as a guest) the person of Gerrit Hooft, serving as third mate on that same ship, detaining him in a chamber guarded by soldiers, having his goods brought ashore, and permitting no one to speak a word with him—a matter truly that has appeared to us as strange as (if it is true, as we do not doubt from the advices) it smacks of tyranny and of the most severe kind that one has heard of or can hear of in the world. For to condemn a man unheard and requesting to be heard, not only to refuse this but to hold him imprisoned, to seize his goods, and moreover to forbid him the conversation of men is of the greatest harshness that one can conceive, and his procedures are entirely intolerable. If Your Excellency had something to say against the aforementioned person, you should have been able to have the court or council convened and assembled, to bring him to justice, to institute fiscal action, and to proceed further according to law, and finally to treat him according to the content of the final sentence based on proof and after proper deliberation. For this reason we request of Your Excellency that the aforementioned Hooft (if such has not been done before the receipt of this) be released from his detention, his goods be restored, and he be permitted to depart with the first ships to Batavia.
